summary: PLuTo is a source-to-source polyhedral framework that finds statement-wise affine transformations with an integer linear program and a bounding cost function, so that rectangular tiling is legal in the transformed space. It emits OpenMP C code with tiled and, where needed, pipelined parallel loops, and reports speedups on six kernels measured on one quad-core shared-memory machine.
why_read: It shows end to end how a polyhedral tool chooses tiling hyperplanes for locality and multicore parallelism, and it is a shared-memory reference point for this survey.
main_contribution: An integer-linear-programming framework with a bounding cost function that finds affine transformations whose hyperplanes allow legal tiling, plus code generation for tiled and pipelined parallel loops over multiple statements.
main_limitation: The paper states that tile sizes were not optimized by any extensive search or model, and its scope is local and shared-memory parallel execution.
evaluation_method: Measured speedups, GFLOPS and run times on one quad-core shared-memory machine against icc and gcc, plus comparisons with Lim-Lam and Griebl transformations forced through the same code generator.

notes: Title differs. Catalog: 'A Practical Automatic Polyhedral Parallelizer and Locality Optimizer'. Title page: 'PLuTo: A Practical and Fully Automatic Polyhedral Program Optimization System'. First author matches (Uday Bondhugula). Year 2008 matches the page footers dated 2008/3/31, but no year is printed on the title page. Author list differs: the catalog lists Bondhugula, Hartono, Ramanujam and Sadayappan, while the title page lists Bondhugula, Ramanujam and Sadayappan with no Hartono. Venue: the catalog gives PLDI 2008, but the PDF is in report form (it calls itself this report), prints no venue, and its only PLDI'08 mention is reference [41], which is a different paper. Correction: the card instruction list omitted analytic-optimization, so the card coded fully-static and static-with-directives. The text describes an integer linear program over a bounding cost function and no programmer annotations, which is the analytic-optimization definition.
